newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia warms to cooperation with eastern Europe.
newsitem.headline: Croatia warms to cooperation with eastern Europe.

text.p: Croatia appeared to soften its opposition on Monday to a United States initiative encouraging economic cooperation among southeastern European countries.

"Croatia is keen to open communications, transport and trade with southeastern Europe and...is ready to take its part of the responsibility for conditions in the neighbouring Balkans," said a statement from the office of President Franjo Tudjman.
The statement followed Tudjman's meeting with John Kornblum, U.S. envoy in the Balkans.

Croatia has previously rejected all U.S. and European Union efforts to boost its cooperation with other former Yugoslav republics, claiming the efforts were aimed at resurrecting the federation from which it seceded in 1991.
The Southeast European Cooperation Initiative (SECI) was initiated by the United States in Geneva in December. It envisages bolstering cooperation among 11 countries.

Croatia and neighbouring Slovenia were the only former Yugoslav republics to refuse preliminary membership in the SECI. Both countries emphasised centuries' old ties with central and Mediterranean Europe instead.
Yugoslavia, now comprising Serbia and Montenegro, was not among the 11 proposed SECI countries, but was expected to be asked to join at a later date.
Kornblum denied outright that SECI was aiming for a loose political union reminiscent of federal Yugoslavia.

"This initiative is in no way seeking to form a new group, alliance, not even a community of nations. It is our effort to view economic, transport and infrastructure issues on a regional basis," Kornblum told independent 101 radio before seeing Tudjman.

"Croatia is an important country, but it's also a small country. Most of the countries of this region are fairly small. There is no way that a true economic infrastructure can be built on national basis," Kornblum added.

Croatian Foreign Minister Mate Granic told reporters that Croatia would give its mind opinion on the initiative only after a meeting in Zagreb on Tuesday with Richard Schifter, U.S. special envoy to the U.N. mission in Geneva.
Schifter, who has fostered SECI, was also scheduled to travel to the Slovenian capital Ljubljana on Tuesday.
"Our president has firmly stated we do not want integration within southeastern Europe, but we do support all aspects of cooperation and normalisation of relations," Granic said.
